standard_prerequisites.name: A normal scheme over a Dedekind domain is flat over it, and a point of a Dedekind spectrum is an effective Cartier divisor
standard_prerequisites.source_reference: More on Algebra, Lemma labelled more-algebra-lemma-dedekind-torsion-free-flat (Stacks tag 0AUW), invoked at proof lines 14686-14687
standard_prerequisites.use: Supplies that the projection of a component dominating S is flat of the required relative dimension, which is what makes the flat pullback a bivariant class in the first case.

standard_prerequisites.name: Flat pullback, proper pushforward and the Gysin map of an effective Cartier divisor as bivariant classes
standard_prerequisites.source_reference: Same chapter, Lemmas labelled lemma-flat-pullback-bivariant (source line 6131), lemma-push-proper-bivariant (source line 6167) and lemma-gysin-bivariant (source line 6149), invoked at proof lines 14689-14692 and 14706-14715
standard_prerequisites.use: Supply the three bivariant operations whose composites c' are capped against classes on Y to realise the cycle level product in each of the two cases.

core_obligations: Define the product on cycles: keep the pairs (i, j) for which X_i or Y_j dominates an irreducible component of S, show that the corresponding X_i x_S Y_j form a locally finite family of closed subschemes of delta-dimension n + m - 1, and form the sum n_i m_j [X_i x_S Y_j]_{n+m-1} (proof lines 14664-14681).

First case: for an integral X' of dimension n dominating an irreducible component of S, use that X' -> S is flat of relative dimension n - 1 to get a bivariant class c' = i_* o (p')^* in A^{-n+1}(X -> S) whose cap product sends [Y'] to [X' x_S Y']_{n+m-1} (proof lines 14684-14698).

Second case: for X' whose composite to S factors through a closed point s, use that s is an effective Cartier divisor with trivial normal bundle, take the Gysin class c in A^1(s -> S), and compose with the flat pullback along X' -> s of relative dimension n to get a class in A^{-n}(X -> S) whose cap product gives the correct cycle when Y' dominates a component of S and zero otherwise, matching the cycle definition (proof lines 14701-14722).
Conclude that the construction factors through rational equivalence in the second variable, and then in the first variable by symmetry (proof lines 14724-14730).
proof_roadmap: Define the product on cycles with the dominance restriction (proof lines 14664-14681).
Build the matching bivariant class in the case where the component dominates S (proof lines 14684-14698).
Build the matching bivariant class in the case where the component maps to a closed point, and conclude by symmetry (proof lines 14701-14730).
difficulty_reason: The statement is that the exterior product map CH_n(X) tensor_Z CH_m(Y) -> CH_{n+m-1}(X x_S Y) over a base of dimension one is well defined (statement lines 14657-14661). The proof first defines the product on cycles: among the pairs (i, j) one keeps only those where X_i or Y_j dominates an irreducible component of S, and shows that these form a locally finite family of closed subschemes of delta-dimension n + m - 1, so that the sum of n_i m_j [X_i x_S Y_j] makes sense (proof lines 14664-14681). Compatibility with rational equivalence is then obtained by splitting the case distinction between components that do and do not dominate S: for an integral X' of dimension n dominating an irreducible component of S, the projection X' -> S is flat of relative dimension n - 1 by the Dedekind domain input, so the composite of the flat pullback with the proper pushforward is a bivariant class whose cap product sends [Y'] to [X' x_S Y']_{n+m-1} (proof lines 14684-14698). For the complementary case, where X' -> X -> S factors through a closed point s of S, the point s is an effective Cartier divisor with trivial normal bundle, so composing the Gysin class of s in S with the flat pullback along the now flat X' -> s of relative dimension n gives a bivariant class whose cap product sends [Y'] to the correct cycle precisely when Y' dominates a component of S and to zero otherwise, matching the definition on cycles (proof lines 14701-14722). Splitting the cycle definition along the two kinds of components and building the matching bivariant class in each case is the non-formal step, so the claim is H2.
